skills.name: Types of fireplaces in a traditional kitchen

note.text:
Three common fireplaces:
• Three-stone fireplace: three stones (or three mounds of earth) hold the pot, with firewood pushed in between. Cheap and simple, but it wastes heat and wood and makes a lot of smoke.
• Improved (mud) stove: a block of mud or clay round the fire with an opening for wood and a hole for the pot, sometimes with a chimney. It keeps the heat in, uses less wood and gives less smoke.
• Charcoal stove (charcoal pot): a metal or clay pot on legs that burns charcoal. Little smoke, easy to carry, but charcoal costs money; never use it in a closed room (carbon monoxide).
Diagrams show how each holds the pot and where the fuel goes.

worked_example.problem: In the drawing, which fireplace is labelled B, and how does it save firewood?
steps: {fireAt(k, 'B') == 'improved (mud) stove' ? 'The mud walls keep the heat round the pot, so less wood is needed' : (fireAt(k, 'B') == 'charcoal stove' ? 'It burns charcoal, not firewood, and keeps the heat under the pot' : 'It does not save wood: heat escapes on all sides')}.

cards.idea: A three-stone fireplace is cheap and simple but wastes heat and gives a lot of smoke.
An improved mud stove keeps the heat in, uses less wood and gives less smoke.
A charcoal stove gives little smoke, but never use it in a closed room.
example: Burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide, a deadly gas.

pick.q: Why must a charcoal stove never be used in a closed room?
pick.r: It gives off carbon monoxide, a deadly gas.
e: It does not wet the room.
pick.y: Carbon monoxide can kill without warning.

pick.q: Why is an improved stove better for health than a three-stone fire?
pick.r: It gives less smoke in the kitchen.
pick.y: Less smoke means healthier lungs and eyes.

misconceptions.explain: Three stones: three-stone fireplace. A block of mud with an opening: improved stove. Metal pot on legs with charcoal: charcoal stove.

solution: Look at what holds the pot and what burns.
